The Bells Toll for Taft
The memorial to Sen. Robert A. Taft which will
be dedicated this morning by President Eisenhower
and former President Hoover is as controversial as
was the Ohio Senator himself. Seldom has a monu
ment so elaborate as the 115-foot Taft bell tower,
the first monument to a member of Congress on
the Capitol grounds, been erected so soon after a
man's death.
No doubt Mr. Taft himself would have relished
the controversy over the Memorial, even on the
occasion of its dedication. He was never afraid of

controversy, and he is perhaps best remembered for
the play of his astringent mind in detecting weak
nesses in the other fellow's argument. As the archtypical Republican, Senator Taft had the courage
of his convictions on a vast range of subjects from
labor legislation to housing. Capable of a curious
insensitivity and blindness along with a neo-isolationism in foreign affairs, he nevertheless sometimes
offset these by a surprising liberalism in domestic
matters and by occasional exercises of great per
ception, as when he saved the country from the
draft of railroad workers demanded by President
Truman.
Yet it is extraordinarily difficult so soon after a
man's death to make an accurate assessment of his
ultimate place in history. The move to build the
bell tower was initiated during the period of public
and congressional shock over Mr. Taft's untimely
death in 1953, seemingly at the peak of his useful
ness, and there was an understandable wish to
memorialize him. Certainly by present judgments
he thoroughly deserves a place in the Senate's "hall
of fame" where his portrait was
hung earlier this
year along with those of four other Senators. But
without detracting in any way from the commemo
ration ceremonies today, we
suggest that they ought
not to set a
precedent for future efforts to prejudge
what only the passage of time and the perspective
of history can make clear.

Washington, D.C, Evening Star, April 14, 1959
In Memory of Sen. Taft
Today President Eisenhower joins in the dedica
tion of the Taft Memorial Bell Tower in Washing
ton, a monument to the memory of Sen. Robert A.
Taft, the idolized "Mr. Republican" of the con
servatives whom Eisenhower defeated for the nom
ination at the 1952 convention.
Sen. Taft was
making his last try for the presi
dency. He had every reason to think his chances
were good. But the internationalists and the "mod
ern
Republicans" teamed up behind Eisenhower,
and Taft was beaten.
That Taft worked for Ike's election in that
campaign was
proof both of Taft's strong character
and of his devotion to Republican party principles.
He stayed in the Senate, working for the ideals
which he believed, for another year, and then he
was dead of cancer.
Sen. Taft's followers often say the country would
have taken a different course if he had been nomi
nated. But in today's perspective Taft's great de
feat came not in 1952 but in 1940.
In the earlier year, had he won the nomination
snatched from him by "meteor" Wendell Willkie,
Taft might have fundamentally altered the course
of history.
In 1940 the New Deal Administration was vul
nerable as at no other time. Leading Democrats
were bitter over the third-term ambition of Frank
lin Roosevelt. Distinguished Americans in both par
ties were
profoundly concerned over the New Deal
foreign policy of taking sides against Hitler and
the Japanese war lords.
Had Taft won out as the Republican candidate
the voters would have had what the Willkie nomi
nation denied them: A clear choice between inter
nationalism and non-intervention. It is more than
likely that the double-barreled weaknesses of the
third term and foreign policy would have defeated
Roosevelt that year.

Twice those in this nation who believed in
Robert A. Taft, and for what he stood raised a
fund.
Once was in 1950. Then the great Ohioan was
marked to be purged from the U. S. Senate because
he had dared to raise his voice against the power
of the labor bosses.
Where the more timid had feared to tread, he

His defense became a crusade. Gifts to help him
poured in from across the nation.
We remember the words spoken so often then:
"I don't always agree with Bob Taft but I always
know where he stands."
That one did, and often in such blunt terms as
to be neither expedient nor popular, as his remark
that a basic principle of law was being violated in
conducting the Nazi war criminal trials under laws
passed after the crimes. What lesser man would
have spoken for a
principle when the country
seethed with emotional hate for the concentration
camp sadists.
The second fund raising came after Bob Taft's
death. It was to build a memorial that posterity
should forever be reminded of him.
Yesterday in Washington the physical part of
that memorial was dedicated as thousands came
forth in April sunshine to see and to hear. When
the bands had ceased to play and the tongues of
his contemporaries had finished their eulogies, the
dulcet voices of the 27 bells in the carillon tower
atop the Taft Memorial sent their music across
Capitol Hill.
It is fitting that the Senator's memorial should
not be mute�
not that there was music in the flat,
Midwestern voice of Bob Taft.
There was no music but there always were facts
and truth, carefully marshalled and courageously
spoken and there never was fear to speak what
needed to be said.
Even 30 days before he died he spoke just as
bluntly about his own impending doom, when he
told Herbert Hoover on July 1, 1953, "My friend,
you know what is the matter with me. I know what
is the matter with me. I'm going to die with my
boots on."
There always will be a need on Capitol Hill for
men who see the truth and who have the courage
to speak it. Let all who hear the bells in the Taft
carillon remember and take heed. That should be
the memorial to Bob Taft and the monument of
stone and metal should be only the symbol and
the reminder.
Let all who hear recall the words of Sen. Styles
Bridges yesterday that "he had no boss but his own
conscience" and of Herbert Hoover that "his con
science was always clear. He lost no sleep at night
worrying that he might be found out."
When the carillon rings, said Mr. Hoover, "it
will be a summons to integrity and courage." And
so it should be if it is to stir a
memory of Bob Taft.

THERE
are a lot of wonderful young
people in this country. I have met them
on not a few university campuses and have
to admit (and really I'm glad to do so)
that they are
leaps ahead of my generation
when we were in school. They impress me
as more mature and better informed. And
while they may demonsti-ate a certain free
dom that we did not, still I think their
general moral tone holds up pretty well.
I'm impressed by then searching ques
tions relative to moral and ethical con
cepts. They reveal a
depth of insight and
earnestness that shows tliey want clear def
initions of right and wrong, of justice and
injustice. Moreover, more of them than
you might think are
trying to live on
high
moral levels and religion is of top interest
on the campus nowadays.
A few years ago I was asked by the
president of my national college fraternity
to serve as chairman of a committee on
morals and manners. I was in for a sur
prise. We wrote to the deans of all the
colleges and universities where the frater
nity is located asking how the local chapter
rated morally and in manners. We told the
deans that we wanted the truth with no
punches pulled. Surprisingly, the great ma
jority replied very favorably. Our commit
tee of old guards was
apparently fearful
that our current active fraternity boys
might be labeled as
being anything from
drunks to educated delinquents.
Well, we should have had more faith in
them. We should have known them better.
Their deans said that basically they are
moral, serious, gentlemanly boys. Their
academic standards are well up and in
most instances they are credited as
being
creative influences in their college com
munities. And the same
report goes for
fraternities generally, not only my own.
The college fraternity is an old institu
tion in American university life. It was
organized in the early days by seriousminded students for the purpose of mutual
helpfulness. Its ritual like those of adult
fraternal orders is based on Biblical back
ground, and the highest idealism is taught
to the brothers at a time and under cir
cumstances of greatest susceptibility.
Fraternities have a much deeper pur
pose than mere
collegiate socializing. On
the wall of one
fraternity house hangs a
picture of the late Methodist Bishop Jo
seph C. Hartzell and below it his words
"Fraternity among men is of God." The
late Vice-President of the United States,
Thomas R. Marshall said, "The forces that
have been greatest in my life have been
God and the college fraternity that molded
me." Such was the emphasis in early days
and this idealism still prevails.
Sometimes we are inclined to take a
negative view of the young, conveniently
forgetting how we ourselves often acted at
the same
age. Don't write them off. They
will probably turn out to be high quality
men and women, solid citizens who in turn
will shake their heads over "the younger
generation."
One day recently I was
looking at my
old college yearbook. It showed a
picture
of my fraternity chapter. One by one I
went down the rows of boys, now
long
since men. I was
impressed to realize that
every one of them had turned out well.
Not a one went bad. As men
they are with
out exception persons of whom to be
proud. Each in his own
way is doing a
worthwhile job in life and all are re
spected, decent men. And believe me some
of them were
"plenty worried about" when
they were in college, including the writer
of this column.
